theme: cultural memory, operational relations and origin narratives
question: Which parts of sophisticated early Indian origin accounts could preserve older practical relations, and which observations could identify their historical route?
outcome: Eighteen source records and 17 observations qualify Manu/Iḍā ritual relations, Rigvedic rivers and DN27's storage-property-authority sequence, with Iranian and transmission controls. The typed graph blocks ten unsupported date transfers and accepts two own-text presence controls. A declared rewrite maps 10,368 invented histories to one account after annotation erasure; retaining route, time, actors or all annotations gives 4, 108, 24 or 10,368 outputs. Developed practical retention and changing-origin mechanisms, plus an explicitly post-audit narrative-reset hypothesis. No diagnostic Harappan memory chain was identified.
challenge: Narrated time, composition, witnesses and physical river processes can be confused. Parallel digital editions share ancestry. A wrong chapter, an English transcription glitch and a publication-year mismatch required source control. A synthetic erasure construction can be mistaken for empirical redaction or complexity generation.
remedy: Preserved failed/corrected acquisitions; checked exact Sanskrit/Pali loci; kept river reaches and access scope separate; corrected Allon to 2022 and confined the manuscript control to its Gāndhārī discourse variant. Independent enumeration and graph reproduction confirm the stated constructions. Prospective tests compare branches, recoverable procedure signatures, specific river configurations and reset accounts.
retry_when: Independent textual branches or material assemblages test a predeclared rare relation bundle and intermediate carrier. Compare operational and attribution changes with shared ancestry and genre controls; use independent identity and composition constraints for any river-event test.
